$comment: FULL-AWS profile. Everything (api + db + worker) runs on the EC2 instance.
THE ONE PIECE OF ARITHMETIC THAT MATTERS:
requests/min  ~=  1.1 x capacity / checkIntervalMinutes
capacity is here; checkIntervalMinutes is a SETTING in the database, edited
on the Settings page. Both are needed — capacity alone bounds the catalogue,
not the rate. 50 products at a 1-minute interval is 55 req/min; the same 50
at 12 minutes is 4.6. Same capacity, twelve times the traffic.
Measured on this address:
4.6/min  (50 @ 12 min)  - the target. 97.7% success observed at 4.4/min.
11  /min  (50 @  5 min)  - blocked every ~3.5 h; 18 of 24 h spent paused.
AWS publishes its own IP ranges, so this address is known to be a datacenter
and is treated accordingly. Run `ramp` before raising anything here.

connection.$comment: A datacenter line, not a household. Silences the home-pool warning.

$comment: 48 identities for 50 products means each makes ~1.2 requests per minute —
slow enough to be a plausible person. Capacity is count x (60000/avg gap) =
72/min against ~56/min of demand.
Ceilings set from what this address has actually been observed to do,
not from what would be convenient:
4.4/min  sustained  -> 97.7% success over 6 h, 3 isolated identity blocks
~11/min  sustained  -> hard block roughly every 3.5 h (6 pauses in 24 h)
25-90/min bursts    -> hard block within a minute
maxPerMin was 90, and that number was never evidence — it was headroom
in case the IP turned out tolerant. It did not. A ceiling is not a target,
but AIMD probes toward it whenever demand is there, so a ceiling nobody
has justified is a wall the controller will eventually walk into. 10 sits
just above the highest rate this address has held cleanly.
This bounds the DAMAGE, it does not set the rate. What sets the rate is
products / interval — see limits.capacity and the check interval.

diurnal.$comment: OFF: 24/7 flat rate, by request. This is the most machine-like property traffic can have — set true if blocking climbs.

tiers.$comment: OFF: all 50 products polled every minute regardless of whether their price moves. Raising these is the cheapest lever if the IP pushes back.

$comment_noiseRatio: Fraction of fetches that browse a homepage/search page INSTEAD of a product (replaces, does not add).
$comment_funnelRatio: Fraction of product fetches that arrive via a search results page. ADDS one request each — already counted in the arithmetic above.
$comment_maxConcurrent: 56/min is ~0.93/s; at up to 8s per fetch that needs ~7.5 in flight. 10 gives margin without bursting.

$comment: capacity caps what is SCRAPED; maxProducts caps what is STORED.
Track as many products as you like — maxProducts 0 means the catalogue is
unlimited. The top `capacity` of them by priority (1 = first) are the ones
the scheduler spends requests on; the rest wait, and are shown as
'waiting on priority' rather than silently going stale.
Why 50: requests/min is roughly 1.1 x products / interval, and 4.4/min is
the rate this address has actually held at 97.7% success. 50 products at a
12-minute interval is 4.6/min — the same traffic Amazon already tolerates,
just spread over a bigger catalogue. Raise it only against a `ramp` number.
A slot frees the moment its holder stops being active, so an auto-paused
listing hands its slot to the next product down rather than holding it.
